title: Not by matted hair (391–400)
hookLine: not matted hair nor family makes one noble, but truth and goodness; the one who owns nothing and clings to nothing
last: BRAHMANA — NOBILITY IS SOMETHING YOU DO.

cards: Everyone wears badges. A uniform, a lanyard, a ring, the right sneakers, the reading list on the coffee table.
Spiritual life has them too: beads on the wrist, the right vocabulary, a meditation app streak you'd rather people noticed.
In the Buddha's India, some holy men wore theirs as hair grown long and matted, and a robe of animal skin. Today's verses look straight at the badge.

teach.h: NOT BY PLATTED HAIR, FAMILY OR BIRTH.
teach.b: Verse three hundred ninety-three, in Max Müller's English: "A man does not become a Brahmana by his platted hair, by his family, or by birth; in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is blessed, he is a Brahmana."
Platted, or matted, hair was the sign of a certain kind of ascetic in ancient India, many of them devoted, serious people. The verse isn't mocking them. It's saying the sign isn't the thing.
The next verse says it more sharply, to someone vain about his look: what use is your matted hair, what use your robe of goatskin?
The inside is a tangle, and you're polishing the outside. Then the real thing, and the picture is surprising.

teach.h: RAGS, VEINS, ALONE IN THE FOREST.
teach.b: The one this chapter honors might wear rags from a rubbish heap, be thin enough that you can see the veins, and sit alone in the forest, meditating. No badge at all. One verse plays on how people spoke.
A man may be born to the right mother and greet others with the polite 'sir' of his class, but if he owns and clings to plenty, that doesn't make him a brahmana.
The brahmana owns nothing and clings to nothing.

The portrait keeps filling in: the one who has cut every fetter and trembles at nothing; who bears insults, blows and even chains without anger, whose patience is an army; free of anger, faithful in duty, keeping the precepts, tamed.
The book has said this before, about the robe, the shaved head and gray hair. Now it says it about the matted hair. The sign isn't the point.

how: Buddhist monastics wear a simple robe and shave their heads, and teachers often use these verses to warn that the robe itself is not the practice; the rag-robe ideal lives on in some forest traditions.

o: a shaved head, the mark of a new monk
a rag robe pulled from a rubbish heap
matted hair, a sign some ascetics wore

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.
p: worn by the one the chapter honors
like an army, says the text

s: verse 393 mocks all ascetics with matted hair
it says the sign isn't the thing; truth and goodness are.
the one the chapter honors owns nothing and clings to nothing
not the one with plenty, even if people call him sir.
these verses praise bearing insults and blows without anger
the brahmana bears them, and his patience is an army.

games.q: two people arrive at a monastery: one with long matted hair and a goatskin robe, one in rags, quiet and kind. whom does this chapter call a brahmana?
o: the one with the matted hair.
the one with truth and goodness in them.
games.why: verse 393: not by platted hair, family or birth; the one in whom there is truth and righteousness is a brahmana.

practice: Think of one badge you wear, spiritual or otherwise, something you like people to notice: a phrase, a thing you own, a streak you keep. Hold it lightly, then imagine setting it down beside you for this sit.
What's left is breath, a body, attention; notice that nothing essential went missing, and rest there with no badge at all.

wordCard.voice: Jaṭā. Matted hair, the sign of some ascetics: the sign isn't the thing, since truth and goodness make one noble, not the look of holiness.

orig.note: Pali jaṭā: matted hair, the sign of some ascetics; verse 393 says it doesn't make one noble.

carryVoice: Your line: not by the hair. Truth and goodness don't need a badge. Two hundred twenty-six days, and counting.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
